newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian prosecutor calls for sex case judge to go.
newsitem.headline: Belgian prosecutor calls for sex case judge to go.

text.p: The magistrate leading investigations into Belgium's child sex abuse scandal should be removed from the case because he accepted a plate of spaghetti from a support group for the families of missing children, the country's top prosecutor said on Wednesday.

Defence efforts to take the case away from Magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte and public prosecutor Michel Bourlet have stirred an additional storm of protest in a country where the legal system is widely believed to have failed badly over the the kidnapping, sex abuse and killing of children.
The Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court, will decide next Monday. But top prosecutor Eliane Liekendael told the court Connerotte was legally compromised by a free meal.
"I am sorry and I regret it, but the law requires his removal," she said. "If only it was possible to find a law to avoid his removal. But I have not found one."
The court does not have to follow her advice.

Magistrate Connerotte and public prosecutor Michel Bourlet are accused by lawyers for two of the 13 people charged in the affair of having shown bias by accepting a meal from a group specialising in helping the parents of missing children.
Four girls have been found dead since mid-August on properties linked to Marc Dutroux, the chief suspect.
The body of an accomplice whom Dutroux admits killing has also been found, and police are searching for at least seven other missing children.

There have been marches in support of Connerotte and Bourlet through the streets of Neufchateau, the centre of the investigations, and a petition against their removal from the case has already attracted 125,000 signatures.
Julien Pierre, the lawyer who was the first to lodge the formal complaint against Connerotte, has received death threats by telephone.
Pierre represents Dutroux who has been charged with murder, abduction and illegal imprisonment.
Virginie Baranyanka, a lawyer representing Jean-Michel Nihoul, another key suspect in the affair, has joined Pierre in his bid to get Connerotte removed.
Whether or not the Cour de Cassation upholds the complaint against Connerotte, the early lodging of the motion for his removal opens the way for an appeal to the Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

An appeal could add years to the case, much to the annoyance of ordinary Belgians who are deeply uncomfortable at the glare of adverse international publicity the case and its revelations of police bungling -- or worse -- has shone on the country.
